overview:
What began in 1933 as the legal exclusion of Jews from German life — boycotts, dismissals, the Nuremberg Laws, the violence of Kristallnacht in 1938 — became, after the German invasion of Poland in 1939 and of the Soviet Union in June 1941, a continent-wide programme of murder. Roughly six million Jews were killed by Nazi Germany, its Axis partners and local collaborators. About 2.7 million died in the killing centres of occupied Poland, above all Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Bełżec and Sobibór; a further 800,000 to a million died of starvation and disease in ghettos and camps. But close to two million were shot, at more than 1,500 sites, in what is often called the Holocaust by bullets — a phase of the killing that came first and that unfolded not behind fences but in fields, ravines and forests within sight and earshot of neighbours.

Almost every event this dataset holds belongs to that shooting phase, and to the summer and autumn of 1941. Within a day of taking Białystok on 27 June, men of Order Police Battalion 309 killed some two to three thousand Jews and locked several hundred inside the Great Synagogue before setting it alight. In August, Einsatzkommando units and their auxiliaries marched roughly 1,400 Jews of the small town of Tykocin into the Łopuchowo forest and shot them into prepared pits over two days; on 26–28 August, at Kamianets-Podilskyi in Ukraine, Friedrich Jeckeln's forces reported killing 23,600 people, the first massacre on that scale and a threshold moment in the turn toward total annihilation. On 29–30 September, at the Babyn Yar ravine outside Kyiv, 33,771 Jews were killed in two days by SS and police units. The murders were not German alone: after a bomb destroyed the Romanian headquarters in Odessa on 22 October, Romanian troops in the Transnistria Governorate shot, burned and hanged tens of thousands of Jews, and drove survivors into ghettos and death marches over the following winter.

The killing was administered as well as improvised, and it followed the ordinary machinery of a modern state — railways, census records, police rosters, camp bureaucracies. Two of the dataset's entries show that machinery at close range. The massacre at Budy in 1942 was carried out inside the Auschwitz system, where a punishment subcamp for women ended in a mass killing by kapos and guards. And in 1943, after the Białystok ghetto was liquidated, some 1,200 of its children were taken to Theresienstadt, kept apart, fed and clothed, and told they were bound for exchange abroad; in October they were put on a train to Auschwitz and gassed on arrival. None survived.
significance: The Holocaust is the reference point against which the modern world measures atrocity: it produced the word genocide, the Nuremberg trials and the legal category of crimes against humanity, the 1948 Genocide Convention and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and it shaped the founding of Israel and the postwar politics of memory across Europe. It also demonstrated something that continues to unsettle: that mass murder on this scale required not fanatics alone but clerks, railway schedulers, middle-aged reserve policemen and cooperative local authorities, and that it happened in public, in towns where the killers and the killed had been neighbours. The sites in this story — Babyn Yar, Odessa, Kamianets-Podilskyi — sat for decades under Soviet memorial language that named the dead as Soviet citizens rather than as Jews, and the struggle to recover who was actually killed there remains an active, and politically charged, undertaking.
coverage: Written from the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's encyclopedia and Britannica, plus reference material on the individual massacres; the seven events beneath this story are drawn almost entirely from 1941 mass shootings in occupied Poland and Ukraine, so the camps and killing centres, the ghettos, the Hungarian deportations of 1944, the death marches, and the Jews of Western Europe, Greece and North Africa are barely represented here. The wider record is uneven in a way no map can fix: German units destroyed nearly all shooting reports before the war ended, so many death tolls rest on perpetrators' own inflated or rounded operational reports, on postwar demographic reconstruction, and on a small number of survivor accounts — at Tykocin, fewer than twenty people. Totals for sites like Babyn Yar, used for later killings as well, are estimates rather than counts.
